chunks: From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Bukayr, from Umar ibn Yazeed, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Dinars with dinars, with one of them being lead, weighed equally by weight.' He said, 'Repeat.' I repeated. Then he said, 'Repeat.' I repeated to him. Then he said, 'I see no harm in it.'

key_terms.الدَّرَاهِمُ: Dinars (gold coins) or silver coins, used here to represent currency in exchange
key_terms.الرَّصَاصُ: Lead, representing a different metal/coin type in the exchange
key_terms.بِوَزْنٍ: By weight, indicating the method of valuation for the exchange
key_terms.لَا أَرَى بِهِ بَأْسًا: I see no harm in it, a common juristic phrase indicating permissibility

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on exchanging coins of different materials by weight in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the application of the riba prohibition in currency exchange, specifically addressing the case where one coin is pure and the other is mixed with lead (rass), ruling it permissible if exchanged by equal weight. The Imam’s repeated request for the question to be repeated highlights the scholarly emphasis on precision in distinguishing between 'gold for gold' and 'silver for silver' categories versus mixed alloys, a key point in Usul al-Fiqh regarding the effective cause (illah) of riba. This ruling supports the view that the strict prohibition applies primarily to homogeneous metals, allowing flexibility in mixed-metal transactions when weight is preserved.
